cards.front: How do glucocorticoids produce their slow, gene-mediated effects?
cards.back: The steroid enters the cell and binds a high-affinity cytoplasmic glucocorticoid receptor. The activated complex moves into the nucleus, binds glucocorticoid response elements and alters transcription, so protein synthesis changes. This takes roughly 30 to 60 minutes, and the effects last longer than the drug because the proteins it switches on persist. A few fast actions, such as suppression of ACTH release, may work through membrane receptors instead.

cards.front: Which oral doses are roughly equal in anti-inflammatory effect to 20 mg of hydrocortisone?
cards.back: Prednisolone 5 mg, methylprednisolone 4 mg, triamcinolone 4 mg, deflazacort 6 mg, and dexamethasone or betamethasone 0.75 mg. Relative to hydrocortisone, dexamethasone and betamethasone are about 25 times as potent as anti-inflammatory agents and have practically no salt-retaining action.

cards.front: Why is DOCA not given by mouth, and what is it used for?
cards.back: DOCA is almost purely mineralocorticoid, but it is not effective when swallowed, so it is given sublingually or by intramuscular injection. It is used occasionally for replacement in Addison's disease.

cards.front: Classify the systemic glucocorticoids by biological duration.
Classify the mineralocorticoids.
cards.text: {{Fludrocortisone}} is orally active and has some glucocorticoid action; {{DOCA}} is an almost pure mineralocorticoid given parenterally or sublingually; {{aldosterone}} is the most potent natural one but is not used clinically because of poor oral bioavailability.

cards.front: Compare hydrocortisone with prednisolone for duration and glucocorticoid potency.
cards.back: Hydrocortisone is short acting and has glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid activity of roughly equal strength, so it is also the replacement drug in adrenal insufficiency. Prednisolone is about four times as potent as a glucocorticoid and has an intermediate duration, which makes it suitable for alternate-day or single-morning dosing.

cards.front: What distinguishes deflazacort from prednisolone?
cards.back: Deflazacort is a slightly less potent glucocorticoid than prednisolone (6 mg is roughly 5 mg prednisolone) and lacks mineralocorticoid activity. It is claimed to cause fewer adverse effects, but this may simply reflect its lower potency. Some trials found less growth retardation in children, so it has been recommended for paediatric patients. It is used mainly for inflammatory and immunological disorders.

cards.front: Short note: Anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressant actions of glucocorticoids

points: Suppress inflammation whatever the cause
Palliative: the underlying disease keeps progressing
Induce annexins, which block phospholipase A2 and so reduce prostaglandins, leukotrienes and PAF
Suppress COX-2 and genes for cytokines such as IL-1, IL-2 and TNF
Reduce adhesion molecules, leukocyte recruitment and capillary leak
Cell-mediated immunity (T cells) is suppressed more than antibody production
Basis for use in autoimmune disease and transplantation
Impair defence against infection
Delay wound healing and can mask a perforating peptic ulcer

cards.front: Short note: Choosing a glucocorticoid by potency, duration and mineralocorticoid activity

points: Pick the agent by the job: replacement, anti-inflammatory, or special site of action
Hydrocortisone: short acting, glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid effects about equal, so it covers both needs
Prednisolone: about four times as potent as hydrocortisone, intermediate duration, suits single-morning or alternate-day dosing
Alternate-day dosing limits HPA suppression
Dexamethasone or betamethasone: long acting, little salt retention, preferred in cerebral oedema; given in late pregnancy for fetal lung maturation
DOCA: mineralocorticoid activity only; fludrocortisone: potent mineralocorticoid with some glucocorticoid activity

cards.front: What is fludrocortisone used for?
cards.back: It is an orally active, potent mineralocorticoid with some glucocorticoid action. Uses: replacement in Addison's disease when sodium is still being lost, salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia, and idiopathic postural hypotension.

cards.front: What is the first-line emergency treatment for acute adrenal insufficiency?
cards.back: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV as a bolus, then given by continuous infusion (KDT: about 100 mg every 8 hours; GG14: 50 to 100 mg every 8 hours). IV isotonic saline with glucose is given, with the volume guided by central venous pressure because these patients handle a water load poorly; a short vasopressor infusion may be needed. Dexamethasone is an alternative (KDT gives 8 to 16 mg IV; GG14 suggests 4 mg when the diagnosis is not yet confirmed, because it does not interfere with the cortisol assay). The precipitating cause (infection, trauma, haemorrhage) must be treated.

cards.front: Complete the list of adverse effects of prolonged glucocorticoid use.
cards.text: Glucocorticoids cause {{hyperglycaemia}}, {{osteoporosis of the vertebrae}}, {{avascular necrosis of the femoral head}}, {{posterior subcapsular cataract}} and {{delayed wound healing}}.

cards.front: Complete the list of relative contraindications to systemic corticosteroids.
cards.text: Relative contraindications include {{peptic ulcer}}, {{diabetes mellitus}}, {{hypertension}}, {{viral and fungal infections}}, {{osteoporosis}}, {{herpes simplex keratitis}}, {{psychosis}}, {{epilepsy}}, {{heart failure}} and {{renal failure}}.

cards.front: Why are dexamethasone or betamethasone preferred over prednisolone in cerebral oedema?
cards.back: They have little sodium-retaining activity, so they do not worsen fluid retention when brain swelling must be controlled. Corticosteroids are also useful in oedema from tumours and in tubercular meningitis.

cards.front: What antenatal steroid regimen is used when preterm delivery is expected, and why?
cards.back: Betamethasone 12 mg IM, two doses 18 to 24 hours apart (KDT: betamethasone or dexamethasone 12 mg IM, two doses 24 hours apart), when delivery is expected before 34 weeks. Glucocorticoids speed fetal lung maturation and surfactant production, so respiratory distress syndrome and neonatal death fall. These two steroids are chosen because they cross the placenta well (less maternal protein binding and placental metabolism than cortisol).

cards.front: What is the current role of corticosteroids in septic shock?
cards.back: High-dose corticosteroid therapy for septic shock has been abandoned because it worsens outcome. Low-dose hydrocortisone (100 mg every 8 hours as an IV infusion for 5 to 7 days) is used in patients with relative adrenal insufficiency who respond poorly to fluids and vasopressors. GG14 describes this state as critical illness-related cortisol insufficiency, treated with hydrocortisone 50 to 100 mg every 6 hours or a 10 mg/hour infusion.

cards.front: How does metyrapone work, and how is it used diagnostically?
cards.back: Metyrapone blocks 11-beta-hydroxylase in the adrenal cortex, so cortisol synthesis falls. Pituitary ACTH output rises, and 11-deoxycortisol accumulates and is excreted in urine. The response is used to test whether the pituitary can mount an ACTH response. Related enzyme inhibitors such as ketoconazole are also tried in Cushing's disease when surgery is not an option.

cards.front: Short note: Adverse effects of prolonged systemic corticosteroid therapy

points: Rounded face, dorsocervical fat pad, central obesity with thin limbs
Thin skin, purple striae, easy bruising, hirsutism
Hyperglycaemia; can unmask or worsen diabetes
Protein catabolism; high-protein, high-potassium diet advised beyond 2 weeks
Osteoporosis of vertebrae; avascular necrosis of femoral head
Proximal myopathy; growth retardation in children
Posterior subcapsular cataract and glaucoma
Peptic ulcer, infections, latent TB flaring, mood change or psychosis

cards.front: Short note: HPA axis suppression and steroid withdrawal

points: Exogenous steroid suppresses the hypothalamo-pituitary-adrenal axis
Adrenal cortex atrophies with time; depends on dose and duration
More than about 20 to 25 mg/day hydrocortisone, or 5 mg/day prednisolone, for over 2 to 3 weeks
Malaise, fever, anorexia, nausea, postural hypotension, electrolyte upset, myalgia
Original disease may flare; stress can precipitate adrenal crisis and collapse
Taper gradually in weekly steps, with smaller steps near physiological dose
Cover stressful events for up to a year after stopping
ACTH does not hasten recovery

cards.front: Short note: Relative contraindications and precautions with corticosteroids

points: Peptic ulcer, diabetes, hypertension, heart failure, renal failure
Viral and fungal infections, tuberculosis, herpes simplex keratitis
Osteoporosis, psychosis, epilepsy
Use only when the benefit justifies the risk, as they may be life-saving
Do not stop abruptly after 2 to 3 weeks
Increase the dose during infection, trauma or surgery
Use local routes (topical, inhaled, intranasal, intra-articular) where possible
Enzyme inducers such as phenytoin and phenobarbitone increase steroid clearance

cards.front: Short note: Replacement therapy in chronic adrenal insufficiency and congenital adrenal hyperplasia

points: Oral hydrocortisone is the mainstay, typically about 20 mg in the morning and 10 mg in the afternoon
Add fludrocortisone if the patient still loses sodium
Adequate salt and water intake
Intravenous hydrocortisone with saline and glucose
Vasopressor if needed
Most often a 21-hydroxylase deficiency
Hydrocortisone suppresses ACTH drive and the excess androgens
Fludrocortisone added for salt wasting

cards.front: Short note: Topical corticosteroids

points: Systemic and topical corticosteroids have one of the widest ranges of medicinal use, for anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive action

cards.front: Essay: Systemic corticosteroids in non-endocrine disease

points: Empirical and largely palliative, but can be life-saving
Aim for the lowest effective dose and shortest course
A single high dose is usually harmless
Start high in severe disease, then taper once symptoms settle
Give extra cover during stress
Rheumatoid arthritis: only severe cases, as an adjuvant to NSAIDs, for exacerbations or systemic features
SLE, polyarteritis nodosa, dermatomyositis, nephrotic syndrome and glomerulonephritis often need steroids
Short courses in urticaria and serum sickness; adrenaline remains the first drug in anaphylaxis
Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia and idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura respond
Asthma: inhaled steroids first; systemic courses for status asthmaticus or exacerbations
Under antimicrobial cover: severe TB (miliary, meningeal), severe lepra reaction, some bacterial meningitis, Pneumocystis pneumonia with hypoxia in AIDS
Cerebral oedema, Bell's palsy, MS relapse, neurocysticercosis
Lymphoid leukaemias and lymphomas; transplant rejection with other immunosuppressants

cards.front: Essay: Adverse effects of long-term glucocorticoid therapy and how to limit them

points: Adverse effects are exaggerations of the pharmacological actions
Limit them mainly through duration and dose
Sodium and water retention, oedema, hypokalaemic alkalosis, rising BP
Less common with the more selective agents
Hyperglycaemia, central obesity, skin fragility, proximal myopathy
Osteoporosis, vertebral fracture, avascular necrosis
Cataract, glaucoma, growth retardation in children
Infections and TB flare; delayed healing
Peptic ulcer risk roughly doubles; bleeding or silent perforation
Euphoria, insomnia, mood change; rarely psychosis or depression
Lowest dose, shortest course, single morning dose
Alternate-day therapy with a short-acting agent when possible
Topical routes; calcium, vitamin D or bisphosphonates for bone
Monitor the HPA axis and withdraw gradually

cards.front: Which enzyme converts testosterone to dihydrotestosterone, and why does DHT matter?
cards.back: 5-alpha reductase converts testosterone to DHT, which binds the androgen receptor more tightly. DHT mediates androgen action on the external genitalia, prostate, genital skin and hair follicles, while testosterone itself mediates feedback inhibition of LH, effects on muscle, erythropoiesis and spermatogenesis. Type 2 5-alpha reductase predominates in the urogenital tract and genital skin, which is why finasteride (mainly type 2) shrinks the prostate.

cards.front: Why is free testosterone not given orally or as a simple injection?
cards.back: Oral testosterone is inactivated by first-pass hepatic metabolism, and a plain intramuscular dose lasts only minutes to hours. Slowly released esters given intramuscularly last weeks, and oral testosterone undecanoate is absorbed through lymphatics, bypassing the liver.

cards.front: What does finasteride do, and how is it used?
cards.back: It is a competitive inhibitor of 5-alpha reductase, mainly type 2, which lowers DHT in the prostate. It shrinks the prostate and improves urinary flow in benign prostatic hyperplasia, but benefit takes about 6 months. It works best in large glands, and 1 mg daily can help male-pattern baldness. Typical side effects are reduced libido, impotence and lower ejaculate volume.

cards.front: Complete the note on anabolic steroids.
cards.text: Anabolic steroids include {{nandrolone}}, {{oxymetholone}}, {{stanozolol}} and {{methandienone}}. Their anabolic selectivity is only modest, and the 17-alkyl ones, such as oxymetholone and stanozolol, can cause {{cholestatic jaundice}} and adverse lipid changes.

cards.front: Classify the antiandrogens and related agents.
cards.text: {{Cyproterone acetate}} is a progesterone-related steroid antagonist; {{flutamide}} and {{bicalutamide}} are nonsteroidal androgen receptor blockers; {{finasteride}} inhibits 5-alpha reductase type 2; {{GnRH agonists}} suppress gonadal androgen output.

cards.front: Which androgens cause cholestatic jaundice, and why are injectable esters preferred?
cards.back: The 17-alkyl derivatives such as methyltestosterone, fluoxymesterone, oxymetholone and stanozolol cause dose-related cholestatic jaundice, which reverses when the drug is stopped. Parenteral testosterone esters do not cause this, so they are preferred for long-term replacement.

cards.front: How does cyproterone acetate reduce androgen action, and what is it used for?
cards.back: It is a weak androgen receptor blocker related to progesterone. Its progestational action suppresses LH, which lowers testosterone and adds to the direct antiandrogen effect. Uses include precocious puberty, inappropriate sexual behaviour in men, and acne or hirsutism in women, given with an estrogen. Hepatotoxicity limits its use.

cards.front: Why is flutamide given together with a GnRH agonist in metastatic prostate cancer?
cards.back: Flutamide is a nonsteroidal androgen receptor blocker, but blocking feedback raises LH and testosterone, which partly offsets it, so monotherapy is poor. It is therefore used with a GnRH agonist or after orchidectomy (combined androgen blockade). KDT advises starting it about 3 days before the agonist to block the initial testosterone flare. Its main toxicity is hepatic; gynaecomastia and breast tenderness are common, while libido and potency are largely preserved. Bicalutamide is now preferred: once daily and less hepatotoxic.

cards.front: Short note: Adverse effects and contraindications of androgen therapy

points: Hirsutism, acne, menstrual disturbance and deepening voice in women
Voice change may be permanent after prolonged use
Gynaecomastia through conversion to estradiol; DHT does not cause it
Oligozoospermia and testicular atrophy with prolonged use
Frequent painful erections early in therapy
Salt and water retention and oedema
Lower HDL and higher LDL, especially with 17-alkyl compounds
Hepatic tumours with long-term oral use
Carcinoma of prostate or male breast, pregnancy, liver or kidney disease
Coronary artery disease, heart failure, men over 65
Can worsen sleep apnoea, migraine and epilepsy

cards.front: Short note: Anabolic steroids

points: Build muscle and bone: nitrogen, minerals and water are retained
The muscle-building effect of exogenous androgens is more marked in women and children than in adult men
Nandrolone, oxymetholone, stanozolol and methandienone: higher anabolic and lower androgenic activity
Replacement in hypogonadism
AIDS-related muscle wasting: testosterone improves weakness
Dose-dependent cholestatic jaundice with 17-alkyl compounds such as oxymetholone and stanozolol
Parenteral testosterone esters do not cause it

cards.front: Short note: testosterone preparations and routes

points: Testes make 5-12 mg testosterone a day; part becomes the more active DHT
About 98% of circulating testosterone is bound to SHBG and albumin
Propionate 25-50 mg i.m. daily to twice weekly (short acting)
Enanthate and decanoate: long acting esters; Sustanon 250 contains 100 mg decanoate, given i.m. every 3-4 weeks
Undecanoate capsule 40 mg, absorbed via lymphatics, bypassing the liver
Dihydrotestosterone gel 25 mg/g once daily on non-scrotal skin

cards.front: Which newer drugs block androgen action in advanced prostate cancer, and how?
cards.back: GnRH antagonists (degarelix by injection; relugolix orally) cut LH, FSH and testosterone quickly without the initial testosterone surge seen with GnRH agonists. Abiraterone acetate inhibits CYP17A1, blocking the synthesis of androgen precursors, and is given with prednisone. Enzalutamide, apalutamide and darolutamide are second-generation nonsteroidal androgen receptor antagonists; enzalutamide binds the receptor 5 to 8 times more tightly than older antiandrogens, and the bound receptor interacts poorly with coactivators and androgen response elements on DNA. These are used with androgen deprivation in metastatic and castration-resistant prostate cancer.

cards.front: Complete the note on PDE-5 inhibitors.
cards.text: The PDE-5 inhibitors used for erectile dysfunction are {{sildenafil}}, {{tadalafil}} and {{vardenafil}}. Of these, {{tadalafil}} has the longest action (half-life about 18 hours), so nitrates are contraindicated for up to {{3 days}} after it, and {{vardenafil}} can prolong the QT interval.

cards.front: What is the physiological mediator of penile erection, and how does it act?
cards.back: Nitric oxide released from nonadrenergic noncholinergic nerves and endothelium raises cGMP in cavernosal smooth muscle, which relaxes it and lets blood fill the sinusoids. Acetylcholine and prostaglandins help. PDE-5 destroys cGMP, which is why blocking it improves erection. This is the base for understanding every ED drug.

cards.front: Name the PDE-5 inhibitors used in erectile dysfunction and state when they work.
cards.back: Sildenafil, tadalafil and vardenafil are first-line drugs. They only enhance the response to sexual stimulation and do nothing without it, because they amplify the nitric oxide signal rather than start it.

cards.front: Why must nitrates never be combined with sildenafil?
cards.back: Both raise cGMP in vascular smooth muscle, so the combination can cause a precipitous fall in blood pressure and myocardial infarction. A gap of 24 hours is needed after sildenafil, and up to 3 days after tadalafil.

cards.front: Short note: Sildenafil, mechanism, adverse effects and interactions

points: Selective PDE-5 inhibitor in the corpus cavernosum
Raises cGMP and potentiates nitric oxide, so it works only with sexual stimulation
50 mg about 1 hour before intercourse; 25 mg if over 65
Can be increased to 100 mg if ineffective
Headache, flushing, nasal stuffiness, dyspepsia, fall in BP
Blue-green colour discrimination loss (PDE-6); rare non-arteritic ischaemic optic neuropathy
Nitrates: precipitous fall in BP, MI possible; avoid nitrates for 24 hours after sildenafil (longer after tadalafil)
Caution with alpha blockers
CYP3A4 inhibitors such as erythromycin, ketoconazole, verapamil and cimetidine potentiate it
Caution in leukaemia, sickle cell anaemia and myeloma (priapism)

cards.front: How does tadalafil differ from sildenafil?
cards.back: Tadalafil is more potent and longer acting: half-life about 18 hours and duration 24 to 36 hours, with peak levels at 30 to 120 minutes, so onset may be slower. Because of its long action, nitrates are contraindicated for up to 3 days after it (GG14: more than 24 hours, especially with tadalafil). It has lower PDE-6 affinity, so visual disturbance is less frequent, but it can cause back pain. Dose: 10 mg at least 30 minutes before intercourse (maximum 20 mg). It is also approved for pulmonary arterial hypertension.

cards.front: Essay: Drug treatment of erectile dysfunction

points: Inability to attain or keep an erection, common after 65
Vascular, neurogenic, hormonal, drug-induced and psychogenic causes
Nitric oxide from NANC nerves and endothelium relaxes cavernosal smooth muscle via cGMP
PDE-5 breaks down cGMP, so its inhibition enhances erection
PDE-5 inhibitors: sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil
Need sexual stimulation to act; not an aphrodisiac
Intracavernosal alprostadil (PGE1), used for neurogenic and psychogenic cases
Papaverine with phentolamine (PIPE) is now rarely used because of priapism and fibrosis
Androgens only when deficiency is proven
Transurethral alprostadil pellet (MUSE) avoids injection but is less effective
Nitrates contraindicated: 24-hour gap after sildenafil; up to 3 days after tadalafil
Avoid in coronary disease where sexual activity is risky
Monitor for priapism and hypotension

cards.front: How do estrogens act at the cell level?
cards.back: Estradiol binds nuclear estrogen receptors, ERalpha and ERbeta. The receptor dimerises, binds estrogen response elements and changes gene transcription with the help of coactivators or corepressors. ERalpha predominates in uterus, breast, bone and blood vessels, while ERbeta predominates in the prostate and ovary. Some rapid membrane-initiated effects also exist.

cards.front: What is the usual cyclical oral HRT regimen for a woman with an intact uterus?
cards.back: Conjugated estrogens 0.625 mg daily for 3 weeks, then 1 week off. A progestin is added for the last 10 to 12 days of each cycle to protect the endometrium from hyperplasia and carcinoma. Lower estrogen doses of about 0.3 to 0.45 mg are also used now. In women without a uterus, estrogen is given alone.

cards.front: Classify the progestins.
cards.text: Progesterone derivatives: {{medroxyprogesterone acetate}}, {{megestrol acetate}}, {{dydrogesterone}} and {{hydroxyprogesterone caproate}}; newer: {{nomegestrol acetate}}. 19-nortestosterone derivatives, estranes: {{norethindrone (norethisterone)}}, {{lynestrenol}} and {{allylestrenol}}. Gonanes: {{levonorgestrel}}, {{desogestrel}}, {{norgestimate}} and {{gestodene}}.

cards.front: Why is ethinylestradiol used by mouth when natural estradiol is not?
cards.back: Natural estrogens are inactivated by rapid first-pass metabolism in the liver, so oral estradiol is weak and short acting. Ethinylestradiol is metabolised slowly, so it is orally active and more potent, which is why it is used in oral contraceptives and oral hormone therapy.

cards.front: What effects do estrogens have on clotting and lipids?
cards.back: They increase synthesis of clotting factors II, VII, IX and X and lower PAI-1, which raises the thrombotic tendency despite increased fibrinolysis. They lower LDL and raise HDL and triglycerides. They also raise SHBG, TBG and CBG levels in the liver.

cards.front: Short note: Progestins, their actions and clinical uses

points: Converts the estrogen-primed endometrium to a secretory state
Thickens cervical mucus so it is hostile to sperm
Reduces uterine motility and oxytocin sensitivity; supports pregnancy
Lowers the frequency of GnRH pulses
Blunts the mid-cycle LH surge when given early in the cycle
Dysfunctional uterine bleeding: high dose stops bleeding, then cyclic low dose
Endometriosis: suppresses menstruation and ectopic implants
Endometrial carcinoma: palliative in advanced disease
Breast tenderness, bloating, mood change, weight gain
Androgenic 19-nortestosterone types lower HDL
Early pregnancy exposure is best avoided

cards.front: Short note: estrogen preparations and doses by route

points: Conjugated estrogens 0.625-1.25 mg/day; lower doses (0.3-0.45 mg/day) also raise bone density
Ethinylestradiol 0.02-0.2 mg/day for menopausal syndrome; mestranol 0.1-0.2 mg/day, converted to ethinylestradiol
Estriol succinate: 4-8 mg/day initially, then 1-2 mg/day
Estradiol esters i.m.: 2.5-10 mg (benzoate, cypionate, enanthate, valerate)
Vaginal: estriol cream 1 mg/g, 1-3 times daily; dienestrol 0.01% cream
Transdermal estradiol 0.025, 0.05 or 0.1 mg per 24 h; cyclic use with progestin for the last 10-12 days
WHI trial in younger women: 24% more CAD, 40% more stroke and doubled venous thromboembolism with combined HRT

cards.front: Essay: Hormone replacement therapy in postmenopausal women

points: Vasomotor symptoms, urogenital atrophy, sleep disturbance
Premature menopause until the natural age of menopause
Estrogen alone after hysterectomy
Intact uterus: estrogen with a progestin for the last 10 to 12 days of each cycle
Perimenopausal women: cyclic rather than continuous HRT; transdermal HRT may have advantages over oral
Prompt relief of hot flushes and urogenital atrophy
Coronary protection only in early postmenopausal women
Combined HRT raises the risk of breast cancer, venous thromboembolism, MI and stroke in older women
No protection against cognitive decline; dementia risk may rise
Gallstones and migraine
Not the best option; bisphosphonates are preferred, but HRT may be used under 60 years of age
Lowest effective dose, shortest duration, usually under 60 years or within 10 years of menopause
Individualise the decision

cards.front: Why is tamoxifen called a SERM, and where does it act as an agonist?
cards.back: It is an estrogen antagonist in breast tissue and blood vessels, but a partial agonist in uterus, bone, liver and pituitary. Its antiestrogenic action inhibits breast cancer cells and causes hot flushes; its agonist action stimulates the endometrium (hyperplasia, carcinoma risk), improves bone density, lowers LDL and raises the risk of deep vein thrombosis 2 to 3 fold.

cards.front: What is the mechanism of danazol?
cards.back: Danazol is an orally active ethisterone derivative with weak androgenic, anabolic, progestational and glucocorticoid activity. Its main action is suppression of the mid-cycle gonadotropin surge, so ovarian or testicular function falls; it also directly inhibits steroidogenic enzymes (not aromatase). As a 17-alkylated steroid it raises C1 esterase inhibitor levels, so it prevents hereditary angioedema attacks. Other uses: endometriosis (now second line because of androgenic and hepatic adverse effects), menorrhagia and fibrocystic breast disease.

cards.front: Classify the selective estrogen receptor agents.
cards.text: Selective estrogen receptor modulators (SERMs) include {{tamoxifen}}, {{raloxifene}} and {{toremifene}}. {{Fulvestrant}} is a pure antagonist that down-regulates the estrogen receptor, so it is called a selective estrogen receptor down-regulator (SERD).

cards.front: Classify the third-generation aromatase inhibitors.
cards.text: Nonsteroidal, reversible: {{letrozole}} and {{anastrozole}}. Steroidal, irreversible (suicide substrate): {{exemestane}}.

cards.front: How does clomiphene induce ovulation, and what are its main adverse effects?
cards.back: It blocks estrogen negative feedback on the pituitary, so more LH and FSH is released with each pulse; the ovaries enlarge and ovulate if they can respond. Course: 50 mg daily for 5 days from cycle day 5, monthly; if no conception after 1 to 2 cycles the dose may be doubled, and no more than 6 cycles are tried. Adverse effects: polycystic ovaries, multiple pregnancy, hot flushes, gastric upset and vertigo. GG14: letrozole gives a higher pregnancy and live-birth rate than clomiphene in PCOS; KDT notes India banned letrozole for ovulation induction in 2011.

cards.front: What is the tissue profile of raloxifene, and what is it used for?
cards.back: It is an estrogen agonist in bone and lipid metabolism, but an antagonist in breast and endometrium. It prevents postmenopausal bone loss and vertebral fracture and reduces the risk of ER-positive breast cancer. It does not relieve hot flushes, and it raises the risk of venous thrombosis.

cards.front: Why are aromatase inhibitors not used in premenopausal women with functioning ovaries?
cards.back: They block estrogen synthesis from androgens, but functioning ovaries keep making estrogen, so the block is incomplete. They are used in premenopausal women only after ovarian removal or with GnRH suppression. In postmenopausal women, extraglandular aromatisation is the main estrogen source, so they nearly abolish estrogen.

cards.front: What is the textbook mifepristone and misoprostol regimen for medical termination of early pregnancy?
cards.back: Mifepristone 600 mg as a single oral dose, followed 48 hours later by misoprostol 400 microgram orally, up to 7 weeks (49 days from the last menstrual period). This gives over 90 percent complete abortion; mifepristone alone gives 60 to 85 percent. Indian kits give mifepristone as three 200 mg tablets on day 1 and misoprostol as two 200 microgram tablets on day 3. Problems: prolonged bleeding and failed abortion; also cramps, nausea and loose stools.

cards.front: Short note: Mifepristone

points: 19-norsteroid; competitive antagonist with weak partial agonism at progesterone receptors A and B, so called a progesterone receptor modulator
Also has antiglucocorticoid and antiandrogenic activity
Follicular phase: blunts the mid-cycle gonadotropin surge and delays ovulation
Luteal phase or early pregnancy: blocks progesterone support, so the decidua breaks down, hCG falls, the cervix softens and prostaglandin release rises
Termination of pregnancy up to 7 weeks: 600 mg, then misoprostol 400 microgram 48 hours later
Cervical ripening before surgical abortion or induction; induction in intrauterine fetal death
Emergency contraception
Cushing syndrome when the tumour cannot be removed
Oral bioavailability about 25%; metabolised by CYP3A4; half-life 20 to 36 hours
Prolonged bleeding, failed abortion, cramps, nausea, loose stools
Avoid in women on long-term glucocorticoids

cards.front: Short note: Aromatase inhibitors

points: Letrozole and other aromatase inhibitors (AIs)
Established hormonal therapy alongside tamoxifen (a SERM)

cards.front: Short note: Antiandrogens

points: Flutamide and bicalutamide (androgen antagonists)
Prostate carcinoma: combined with GnRH analogue to prevent the initial flare-up of the tumour caused by increased gonadotropin secretion

cards.front: Short note: clomiphene and ovulation induction

points: Nonsteroidal SERM used to induce ovulation
Well absorbed orally, deposited in fat, plasma half-life about 6 days
50 mg once daily for 5 days, starting from cycle day 5
If no conception in 1-2 months, the daily dose may be doubled for 2-3 cycles
Menotropins or hCG added on the last 2 days of the course improves success
Male infertility: 25 mg daily for 24 days a month, with 6 days rest, for up to 6 months

cards.front: Short note: Tamoxifen versus aromatase inhibitors in breast cancer

points: SERM; antagonist in breast, so usable in premenopausal women
Risks: endometrial hyperplasia and cancer, venous thromboembolism
Letrozole and anastrozole (reversible, nonsteroidal); exemestane (irreversible, steroidal)
Only in postmenopausal women, or with ovarian suppression
Better in adjuvant and advanced disease; bone loss and arthralgia
Postmenopausal: tamoxifen is generally replaced by an AI after about 2 years; tamoxifen up to 10 years, or an AI for 5 to 10 years after 5 years of tamoxifen, improves outcomes
Premenopausal: tamoxifen; in high-risk disease exemestane plus ovarian suppression did better than tamoxifen plus ovarian suppression (SOFT/TEXT trials)

cards.front: What is the dose and time window for ulipristal as emergency contraception?
cards.back: Ulipristal 30 mg as a single oral dose, taken within 120 hours of unprotected intercourse. It is as effective as levonorgestrel when taken within 72 hours and more effective than levonorgestrel from 72 to 120 hours. It is a selective progesterone receptor modulator.

cards.front: Complete the note on drug interactions with oral contraceptives.
cards.text: Enzyme inducers such as {{rifampicin}}, {{phenytoin}}, {{phenobarbitone}} and {{carbamazepine}} speed the metabolism of contraceptive steroids and can cause contraceptive failure. The woman should switch to a pill containing {{50 microgram}} ethinylestradiol or use {{another method}} of contraception.

cards.front: Complete the note on long-acting progestin injectables.
cards.text: Depot {{medroxyprogesterone acetate}} 150 mg is given intramuscularly every {{3 months}}; {{norethisterone enanthate}} 200 mg is given every {{2 months}}. The main drawback is disruption of menstrual bleeding or total {{amenorrhoea}}, and return of fertility after stopping is {{delayed by several months}}.

cards.front: Why are desogestrel and gestodene preferred in some combined pills?
cards.back: They are potent gonane progestins with strong antiovulatory action and little or no androgenic activity. Because they are potent, the ethinylestradiol dose in the pill can be reduced. Because they are weakly androgenic, they do not oppose estrogen's favourable effect on the lipid profile, so they are preferred in women with hyperandrogenism. Desogestrel and norgestimate are prodrugs.

cards.front: Short note: Adverse effects and contraindications of combined oral contraceptive pills

points: Nausea, headache, breast discomfort, spotting, mostly in the first cycles
Chloasma, acne or weight gain with older androgenic progestins
Venous thromboembolism and arterial events, greater with age, smoking and older high-dose pills
Blood pressure rise, usually reversing after stopping
Thrombosis or stroke, coronary disease, moderate to severe hypertension
Liver disease, genital or breast cancer, porphyria
Major surgery: stop 4 weeks before
Diabetes, obesity, smoking, age over 35, migraine, mild hypertension, gallbladder disease

cards.front: Short note: Combined oral contraceptive pill - contraindications

points: Thromboembolic disease, coronary and cerebrovascular disease (and other vascular conditions as listed in KDT8)
Estrogens raise biliary cholesterol excretion, so gallstones are slightly more frequent with OCs or long-term use

cards.front: Essay: Oral contraceptive pills: types, mechanism, safety and counselling

points: Reversible suppression of fertility, most widely used method
Fertility returns within 1 to 2 months of stopping
Combined monophasic 21 + 7 pills; phasic pills
Progestin-only minipill taken daily without a break
Emergency pills, injectables, implants, transdermal patch
Main action is suppression of the mid-cycle LH and FSH surge, so no follicle ruptures
Thick cervical mucus and an unfavourable endometrium for implantation
Early nausea, spotting and breast discomfort
Venous thrombosis and arterial events, mainly with estrogen; smoking and age over 35 add risk
Breakthrough bleeding, chloasma, mood change
Absolute: thrombosis, liver disease, genital or breast cancer, impending major surgery
Enzyme inducers such as rifampicin, phenytoin and carbamazepine reduce efficacy
Use a 50 microgram estrogen pill or another method of contraception
One missed pill: take two the next day; if more than 2 are missed, stop the course, use another method and restart with the next cycle
Pregnancy must be excluded if periods stop
Stop at once for symptoms of thrombosis or severe headache

cards.front: How do oxytocin and vasopressin differ?
cards.back: Both are nine-amino-acid peptides made in the hypothalamus and stored in the posterior pituitary, and they differ at positions 3 and 8. Oxytocin acts mainly on the uterus and breast, while vasopressin mainly controls water excretion. Very high doses of oxytocin can show some antidiuretic effect.

cards.front: How does oxytocin stimulate the uterus, and what changes its sensitivity?
cards.back: It acts on G-protein-coupled receptors on the myometrium, raising intracellular calcium through depolarisation and IP3-mediated release. It also stimulates prostaglandin release from the endometrium. Estrogens increase receptor numbers, so sensitivity rises toward term and falls after delivery. Progestins reduce it.

cards.front: How are ergometrine and methylergometrine used to control postpartum haemorrhage?
cards.back: Give 0.2 to 0.3 mg IM at delivery of the anterior shoulder to prevent PPH in women prone to bleed (for example grand multipara, uterine inertia), or 0.5 mg IV if PPH is occurring; in severe bleeding 0.5 mg can be combined with oxytocin 5 IU. Routine use in all deliveries is not justified, and multiple pregnancy must be excluded first. GG14 describes oxytocin 10 units IM immediately after delivery as the standard measure to keep the uterus contracted.

cards.front: What are the obstetric uses of prostaglandins?
cards.back: PGE2, PGF2alpha and 15-methyl PGF2alpha are potent uterine stimulants, especially late in pregnancy, and they also soften the cervix. Misoprostol, a PG analogue with fewer side effects, is increasingly used for obstetric indications such as cervical ripening and induction.

cards.front: Complete the note on ergot alkaloids in obstetrics.
cards.text: Ergometrine and methylergometrine raise the force, rate and duration of uterine contraction, and high doses can cause {{contracture}}. Ergometrine given for many days after delivery can reduce milk through {{dopaminergic inhibition of prolactin release}}.

cards.front: Complete the note on oxytocin pharmacokinetics.
cards.text: Oxytocin is inactive by mouth and is given IM or IV. It is broken down by {{oxytocinase}} from the placenta, with a plasma half-life of about {{6 to 12 minutes}}. {{Carbetocin}} is a long-acting analogue used to prevent uterine atony after caesarean section.

cards.front: Classify the tocolytic drugs.
cards.text: Beta-2 agonists: {{ritodrine}}, {{salbutamol}}, {{terbutaline}}. Calcium channel blocker: {{nifedipine}}. Oxytocin receptor antagonist: {{atosiban}}. {{Magnesium sulfate}} also relaxes the uterus but is no longer recommended for this purpose. COX inhibitors such as {{indomethacin}} are used off-label (GG14), while KDT lists them among unreliable uterine depressants.

cards.front: Which conditions must be checked before starting an oxytocin infusion for induction of labour?
cards.back: Correct presentation, mature fetal lungs, no cephalopelvic disproportion, no placenta praevia, no fetal distress, and no previous uterine scar. The infusion is started slowly and titrated to the response, with contractions monitored closely, and it is stopped once contractions are strong enough.

cards.front: What serious adverse effect of oxytocin is linked to its antidiuretic action?
cards.back: Water intoxication, which can be fatal. It occurs when large doses are given with intravenous fluids, especially in toxaemia of pregnancy and renal insufficiency. Over-strong uterine contractions from injudicious use can also cause uterine rupture and fetal asphyxia.

cards.front: In which conditions should ergometrine be avoided?
cards.back: Hypertension, toxaemia, vascular or cardiovascular disease, sepsis (risk of gangrene), liver or kidney disease, and in pregnancy before the third stage of labour. In hypertensive women, oxytocin is the preferred uterotonic.

cards.front: Short note: Tocolytic drugs

points: Aim: delay labour to allow glucocorticoid therapy for lung maturation or transfer to a better centre; tocolytics delay delivery but have not been shown to improve fetal outcome
Likely to work only if cervix is under 4 cm and the lower segment is barely taken up
Avoid if membranes have ruptured, with antepartum haemorrhage, severe toxaemia, intrauterine infection or fetal death
Ritodrine IV infusion from 50 microgram/min, raised until contractions stop or maternal HR reaches 120/min; not beyond 48 hours
Hypotension, tachycardia, arrhythmia, pulmonary oedema, hyperglycaemia, hypokalaemia
Salbutamol and terbutaline are alternatives
Nifedipine oral, 10 mg repeated once or twice after 20 to 30 minutes, then 10 mg 6-hourly
Efficacy similar to beta-2 agonists with fewer maternal side effects; GG14: more likely to improve fetal outcome
Atosiban IV infusion at 24 to 33 weeks; fewer cardiovascular and metabolic effects
Used in Europe and UK; not approved in USA (KDT: nor in India)
COX inhibitors such as indomethacin: GG14 notes off-label use; avoid beyond 32 weeks (ductus closure); short courses under 72 hours are safer
Magnesium sulfate: first-line for eclampsia seizures; risky as a tocolytic and no longer recommended (KDT)

cards.front: Short note: Oxytocin in labour and postpartum haemorrhage

points: Peptide, so given IV or IM; very short plasma half-life of minutes
Degraded by oxytocinase from placenta and liver
Induction and augmentation of labour
Postpartum haemorrhage and after caesarean section
Breast engorgement from poor milk ejection
Effect can be controlled and stopped quickly
Normal relaxation between contractions preserves fetal oxygenation
Lower segment not contracted, so descent is not hindered
Hyperstimulation, uterine rupture, fetal asphyxia
Water intoxication with large doses and IV fluids

cards.front: Short note: Tocolytic agents (beta-2 stimulants)

points: Salbutamol, terbutaline, salmeterol, formoterol, ritodrine
Selective beta-2 stimulation: bronchodilatation, vasodilatation and uterine relaxation, without significant cardiac stimulation

cards.front: Essay: Uterotonic drugs for postpartum haemorrhage

points: Uterine atony is the main cause of PPH
Uterotonics give sustained contraction that compresses the vessels running through the myometrial mesh
KDT: 5 IU IM or by IV infusion for an immediate response; GG14: 10 units IM after delivery, or 20 units in 1 litre infused at 10 mU/min
Preferred in hypertensive women, in whom ergometrine is contraindicated
0.2 to 0.3 mg IM at delivery of the anterior shoulder; 0.5 mg IV if PPH is occurring
Methylergometrine is more potent on the uterus with milder other actions
Carboprost (15-methyl PGF2alpha) 0.25 mg IM, repeated every 30 to 120 minutes, for atony unresponsive to oxytocin and ergometrine
Carbetocin: long-acting oxytocin analogue for preventing atony after caesarean section and controlling PPH
Choose by blood pressure, uterine tone and urgency
Ergots are avoided in hypertension, toxaemia, vascular disease and sepsis
Nausea, vomiting and BP rise with ergots
Hyperstimulation and water intoxication with oxytocin; monitor uterine tone and bleeding

cards.front: How does dinoprostone (PGE2) help when the cervix is unfavourable at term?
cards.back: Low doses applied in the vagina or cervical canal soften the cervix and make it compliant (cervical priming) without affecting uterine motility. If needed, oxytocin can start labour about 12 hours later, so the chance of induction failure falls.

cards.front: What is the classical bioassay tissue for oxytocin?
cards.back: Isolated non-pregnant rat uterus. Rats are primed with diethylstilboestrol first so the strip responds reliably to oxytocin; this also keeps the uterus quiet but sensitive for routine assays.

cards.front: Short note: Detection and estimation of oxytocin

points: Oxytocin contracts the isolated rat uterus
Unknown samples are estimated by comparing their contraction with a standard dose
Prime rats with diethylstilboestrol: about 36 to 48 h before (Ghosh) or stilboestrol 0.1 mg/kg i.m. 24 h before (Medhi)
Use de Jalon's solution, with a quarter of the calcium of Ringer-Locke
Keep the bath at 25 to 35 C and aerate with O2 plus 5% CO2 to damp spontaneous activity
Doses of about 0.1 to 3 milliunits/ml
Contact for 30 s, with about 5 min between doses
Other smooth-muscle polypeptides are told apart by their responses in different tissues
Histamine-like activity is blocked by mepyramine; 5-HT-like activity by methysergide

cards.front: Why is the oxytocin bioassay run in a low-calcium bath?
cards.back: Calcium increases spontaneous uterine activity and drug sensitivity, so a quarter of the Ringer-Locke calcium keeps the strip quiet and gives cleaner responses. Sensitivity to oxytocin falls slightly, but the gain in steadiness outweighs it.

cards.front: Which eye conditions get topical steroids, and which need systemic therapy?
cards.back: Anterior-segment inflammation such as allergic conjunctivitis responds to eye drops or ointment. Posterior-segment disease (retinitis, optic neuritis, uveitis) needs systemic steroids, or a retrobulbar injection to limit systemic effects. Steroids are contraindicated in herpes simplex keratitis and in ocular injury.

cards.front: Short note: Non-endocrine uses of corticosteroids

points: Inhaled steroid first when a patient needs a beta-2 agonist almost daily
Systemic steroid only for status asthmaticus (IV), acute exacerbations (short high-dose oral course, then taper) or severe chronic asthma uncontrolled by inhalers
Systemic therapy for pemphigus vulgaris, exfoliative dermatitis and Stevens-Johnson syndrome
Posterior-segment eye disease needs systemic steroids
Ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease and coeliac disease with exacerbation
Part of combined chemotherapy for acute lymphatic leukaemia, Hodgkin's and other lymphomas
High-dose steroids with other immunosuppressants to prevent graft rejection; low maintenance doses continued long term
High-dose therapy for septic shock has been abandoned; low-dose hydrocortisone is used for relative adrenal insufficiency

cards.front: Short note: Drospirenone

points: Progestin derived from spironolactone
Antimineralocorticoid and antiandrogenic activity
Combined oral contraceptive: ethinylestradiol 30 µg with drospirenone 3 mg in a 28-tablet monophasic pack
Also combined with estradiol in a hormone replacement product
Antiandrogenic and antimineralocorticoid action may give a cardiovascular advantage over older progestins
Newer progestins of this type are discussed as advances in the contraceptive field

cards.front: Essay: Neuroendocrine control of the menstrual cycle and the role of oral contraceptives

points: Cycle run by hypothalamic GnRH pulses, pituitary FSH and LH, and ovarian estradiol and progesterone
Oral contraceptives suppress this axis so that no ovulation occurs
GnRH is released in pulses and stimulates both FSH and LH
Gonadal steroids feed back on pituitary and hypothalamus; the effect depends on concentration and timing
Follicular phase: estradiol rises under FSH; a preovulatory LH surge triggers ovulation
Luteal phase: corpus luteum progesterone under LH; when support falls the endometrium is shed
Estrogen plus progestin blocks the mid-cycle LH surge, so ovulation does not occur
Potent progestins such as levonorgestrel have a low ovulation-inhibiting dose; the pill holds 2 to 3 times more
Thick cervical mucus hostile to sperm and an unsuitable endometrium add to the effect
Absolute contraindications include thrombosis, stroke and coronary disease
Relative ones include diabetes, obesity and smoking
Enzyme inducers such as rifampin reduce contraceptive effect; with rifampin, advise an alternative method, while other inducers may be met by a pill with 50 µg ethinylestradiol

cards.front: Which animals are used to screen antifertility agents?
cards.back: Rats most commonly; mice, rabbits and monkeys can also be used. Rats are routine because a test running 12 weeks covers every stage of spermatogenesis, which takes about 9 weeks.

cards.front: Essay: Experimental and clinical evaluation of antifertility drugs

points: Screening must show temporary and fully reversible sterility in animals
Rats are routine; mice, rabbits and monkeys can also be used
Ovulation inhibition: ovary weight falls after unilateral ovariectomy and ovarian histology shows changes
Antiestrogenic action: change in uterine weight
Progestational action: deciduoma formation in the uterus
Implantation or early foetal loss: count implants and resorptions
Cohabitation test: treated males mated with fertile females; check sperm in the vagina, pregnancy timing, pseudopregnancy and oestrous cycle
Test over about 12 weeks, because a rat's spermatogenesis takes about 9 weeks; examine epididymal sperm
After satisfactory animal data, an IND application starts human trials through Phase I to III, then an NDA
Failure rates are compared, e.g. about 98 to 99.9% effective for the combined pill versus 96 to 98% for the minipill

cards.front: Short note: Newer progestins in hormonal contraception

points: Potent progestins with strong antiovulatory action and little androgenic activity
Suit women with hyperandrogenism; allow ethinylestradiol to fall to 20 µg
Spironolactone-derived; antimineralocorticoid and antiandrogenic
Ethinylestradiol 20 µg with drospirenone 3 mg in 24 active tablets
Ulipristal, a selective progesterone receptor modulator, 30 mg single dose up to 120 h

cards.front: Essay: Recent advances in hormonal contraceptives

points: Aims: lower hormone dose, same efficacy, fewer metabolic effects
Methods now include pills, implants, injectables and emergency options
Desogestrel, gestodene and norgestimate: prodrugs or potent progestins with little androgen
Drospirenone: antimineralocorticoid and antiandrogenic action
Ethinylestradiol 20 µg is possible when the progestin is strongly antiovulatory
Ormeloxifene, a nonsteroidal SERM, probably works through utero-embryonic asynchrony and failure of implantation
Levonorgestrel implants: six capsules of 36 mg each, active for up to 5 years
Levonorgestrel intrauterine system (52 mg) is approved for contraception and effective for 5 years
Progestin-only levonorgestrel 1.5 mg single dose beats the older Yuzpe regimen
Ulipristal 30 mg up to 120 h
Rifampin and other enzyme inducers reduce efficacy

cards.front: What is ormeloxifene (centchroman)?
cards.back: A nonsteroidal SERM developed in India as an oral contraceptive. It acts as an estrogen antagonist in uterus and breast, has little action on vaginal epithelium or cervical mucus, and probably acts by failure of implantation. Its plasma half-life is about 1 week.

cards.front: Short note: Male contraception

points: Suppress spermatogenesis; sperm take about 64 days to form, so onset and recovery are slow
Gonadotropin suppression lowers testosterone, causing loss of libido and impotence
Estrogens and progestins feminise; men rarely accept regular medication
Testosterone combined with a progestin is not a reliable method
GnRH antagonist with testosterone gave reversible azoospermia in nonhuman primates
Oral nonsteroidal cottonseed compound; reduces sperm motility and suppresses spermatogenesis
Fertility returns months after stopping, but about 10% stay oligozoospermic
Main toxicity is hypokalaemia; use has been dropped

cards.front: What is the most important adverse effect of gossypol?
cards.back: Hypokalaemia from renal potassium loss, causing muscle weakness and occasionally paralysis. Oedema, diarrhoea, breathlessness and neuritis also occur.

cards.front: Short note: Postcoital (emergency) contraception

points: Woman not on regular contraception who had unprotected intercourse
Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg single dose, or 0.75 mg twice 12 h apart, as early as possible and within 72 h
Ulipristal 30 mg single dose within 120 h; as effective as levonorgestrel up to 72 h and better from 72 to 120 h
Mifepristone 600 mg within 72 h interferes with implantation
Levonorgestrel 0.5 mg with ethinylestradiol 0.1 mg, twice 12 h apart within 72 h
Less effective and more nausea (20 to 50%) than the progestin-only regimen (about 6%)
Next period may be delayed or disrupted
Not a routine method

cards.front: What is the Yuzpe method?
cards.back: Emergency contraception using levonorgestrel 0.5 mg with ethinylestradiol 0.1 mg, two doses 12 hours apart, within 72 hours. It is less effective and causes more nausea than the progestin-only levonorgestrel regimen.

cards.front: How do superactive GnRH agonists act, and what does continuous dosing do?
cards.back: They first trigger a brief rise in FSH and LH. After 1 to 2 weeks they desensitise and down-regulate pituitary GnRH receptors, so gonadotropins fall and gonadal steroids drop to castration levels. Recovery takes up to about 2 months after stopping.

cards.front: Classify the GnRH analogues
Why do GnRH antagonists avoid the initial flare seen with agonists?
cards.back: Antagonists block the GnRH receptor directly, so they inhibit FSH and LH secretion without a first stimulatory phase. Ganirelix and cetrorelix are short acting and block LH surges during controlled ovarian stimulation for IVF.

cards.front: Short note: Clinical uses of GnRH agonists and antagonists

points: Depot agonist for androgen suppression; start with flutamide or bicalutamide to cover the initial flare
Endometriosis, uterine fibroids and polycystic ovary: pharmacological castration
Premenopausal breast cancer
Precocious puberty with depot dosing
IVF: agonist or antagonist prevents premature LH surge during ovarian stimulation
Investigational contraceptive use in both sexes
Menopause-like effects: hot flushes, sweating, vaginal dryness, amenorrhoea

cards.front: What does oligozoospermia mean, and how does it arise?
cards.back: The ejaculate carries fewer sperm than normal. When gonadotropin secretion falls short, spermatogenesis is defective and the man has oligozoospermia with male sterility. The defect is in sperm output, not in androgen action as such: androgen replacement brings sexual maturation, while fertility needs gonadotropin therapy. KDT8 also writes of oligo-asthenospermic subfertile men.

cards.front: Short note: drug therapy of oligospermia

points: Sulfasalazine, exogenous androgens and cyproterone acetate can each suppress spermatogenesis; the sulfasalazine effect reverses when the drug is stopped
Gonadotropin deficiency is the group in which drugs can establish or restore fertility; intrinsic gonadal disease responds poorly
hCG is started first to drive testosterone production: 1500 to 2000 IU intramuscularly or subcutaneously three times a week (Katzung gives 1000 to 2500 IU several times a week)
Recombinant FSH (about 150 IU) or hMG 75 to 150 IU three times a week is added if spermatogenesis does not begin on hCG alone
Sperm appear during 4 to 6 months in up to 90% of men, often at subnormal counts; some need up to 2 years
Gynaecomastia is the commonest adverse effect, in up to a third of patients
Clomiphene increases gonadotropin secretion: 25 mg daily for 24 days a month with 6 days rest, for up to 6 months, although success rates are low
Mesterolone is promoted for oligospermia because it suppresses gonadotropins less than testosterone does

A meta-analysis of 11 trials found that oral androgens (mesterolone, testosterone undecanoate) did not improve sperm count, motility or pregnancy rate in oligo-asthenospermic men, so this use lacks evidence
Exogenous testosterone itself lowers gonadotropins and can cause oligozoospermia and testicular atrophy

cards.front: Why is exogenous testosterone the wrong drug for restoring fertility?
cards.back: Spermatogenesis needs a high intratesticular androgen concentration, which is why androgens were expected to help. But exogenous androgen feeds back on the pituitary, LH and FSH secretion falls, and the testis loses its gonadotropin drive. Moderate doses for a few weeks cause oligozoospermia even in men with normal testosterone, and prolonged use causes testicular atrophy. Androgens are therefore used to replace androgen effects, not to restore spermatogenesis.

cards.front: Which drugs cause oligospermia?
cards.back: Sulfasalazine has been reported to cause oligozoospermia and male infertility, and the effect reverses when the drug is stopped. Exogenous androgens suppress gonadotropins and lower sperm output, and cyproterone acetate, a potent progestin and antiandrogen, also produces oligospermia.

cards.front: Why is estrogen not given unopposed to a woman with an intact uterus?
cards.back: Continuous estrogen without a progestin keeps stimulating the endometrium: irregular bleeding follows and the risk of endometrial carcinoma rises 5 to 15 fold, so a progestin is added for the last 10 to 12 days of each month. Estrogen alone is reserved for hysterectomised women or when a progestin cannot be used; low-dose unopposed estrogen is claimed not to raise endometrial cancer risk.

cards.front: Essay: Therapeutic uses of estrogens

points: Estrogens are the ovarian hormones behind the female secondary sex characters and behind endometrial proliferation in the preovulatory phase
Therapeutically they are used either for replacement when ovarian function fails, or in pharmacological doses to suppress the pituitary-gonadal axis
The two commonest uses today are hormonal contraception and hormone replacement therapy; the rest are gynaecological or palliative
Menopausal problems treated: vasomotor symptoms, urogenital atrophy, osteoporosis, skin and psychological changes
Estrogen with or without a progestin relieves hot flushes and atrophic changes promptly; the accepted indication is symptomatic women under 60 years or within 10 years of menopause

Regimen: conjugated estrogens 0.625 mg/day in cycles of three weeks with a one week break, with a trend to 0.3 to 0.45 mg/day; a progestin is added for the last 10 to 12 days in women with an intact uterus
Estrogen alone after hysterectomy; transdermal estradiol is preferred by many; tibolone is an alternative for the same purpose
Osteoporosis: restores calcium balance and stops further bone loss, but bisphosphonates work better and are preferred; HRT is not recommended beyond 5 years or over 60 years of age

Risks: combined HRT increases breast cancer, venous thromboembolism, myocardial infarction and stroke in older women (WHI); it does not protect against cognitive decline and may double dementia; gallstones and migraine are more frequent
Ethinylestradiol with a progestin in combined oral pills; the main action is suppression of the mid-cycle LH and FSH surge, so no follicle ruptures
The older estrogen-containing (Yuzpe) emergency regimen has been overtaken by progestin-only emergency pills, which are better tolerated and two to three times as effective
Estrogen restores the premenopausal vaginal cytology and prevents as well as treats atrophic vaginitis of elderly women
Topical preparations are preferred when local symptoms are the only problem; an antibacterial may be combined
Also relieves kraurosis vulvae and dyspareunia
Ovarian agenesis (Turner syndrome) or hypopituitarism: cyclic estrogen from about 12 to 13 years, raised slowly to adult doses, with a cyclic progestin added later
Treatment is continued until about the age of natural menopause; growth hormone, or a little androgen, can be added to improve height

Dysmenorrhoea: cyclic estrogen with an added progestin inhibits ovulation (anovular cycles are painless) and reduces endometrial prostaglandin synthesis; reserved for severe cases after prostaglandin synthesis inhibitors

Acne: estrogen suppresses ovarian androgen production by inhibiting pituitary gonadotropin release; cyclic treatment with a progestin is effective, but topical therapy is preferred in girls and estrogen is never used in boys
A progestin taken cyclically is the logical and effective therapy; estrogens help only as adjuvants
Palliation only, in both primary and metastatic disease, through pituitary suppression of androgen production
GnRH agonists with or without an antiandrogen are now preferred for this purpose
Contraindicated in pregnancy
Unopposed estrogen causes endometrial hyperplasia and carcinoma, so a progestin is added when the uterus is present
May make an existing breast cancer grow faster; raises the risk of venous thrombosis and of arterial events
Gallstone risk about doubles; benign hepatomas in teenagers and women in their twenties on long-term treatment; worsens migraine, epilepsy and endometriosis
In males causes gynaecomastia, loss of libido and feminisation; in children closes the epiphyses and reduces adult height
